subject: biology
title: Journey Through the Gut
welcome_lead: Follow a bite of apple from your mouth to where it leaves your body.
meta_desc: KS3 Biology adventure on the order of digestion through the gut.
final_note: You can now name the digestive organs in the right order from mouth to bottom.

concepts.def: Where food is chewed and mixed with saliva.
Tube carrying food to the stomach.
Bag where food is mixed with acid.
Long tube where nutrients are absorbed.

walkthroughs.body_html: Food travels: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum. Each part has its own job.
Teeth and saliva start digestion in the mouth. The stomach uses acid to break food. The small intestine absorbs nutrients. The large intestine absorbs water.
Food spends about 1 minute in the oesophagus, 2-4 hours in the stomach, around 4 hours in the small intestine, and up to a day in the large intestine.

mcqs.q: After pre-mRNA splicing in eukaryotes, which sequences remain in the mature mRNA?
options: Ribosomes synthesise amino acids from scratch using the mRNA as a template.
Both introns and exons are removed and the cell uses just the cap and tail.
Introns remain because they encode the protein; exons are removed as junk.
Exons remain; introns are removed.

mcqs.q: What drives water up the xylem in a tall tree?
options: Capillary action alone is enough to lift water to the top of any tree.
Ribosomes synthesise amino acids from scratch using the mRNA as a template.
Roots actively pump water up to the leaves like a heart.
Transpiration pull — evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls water up the continuous water column.

mcqs.q: What reads the mRNA codons during translation?
options: Both introns and exons are removed and the cell uses just the cap and tail.
Ribosomes synthesise amino acids from scratch using the mRNA as a template.
tRNA molecules carrying specific amino acids — their anticodons pair with mRNA codons at the ribosome.
DNA directly reads the codons on mRNA and adds amino acids.
